scoreNote: Strong (5): a balanced reading that grants posterity's perspective while showing that contemporaries often see greatness clearly and that later ages bring distortions of their own; well organized and thoughtful.

sentences.text: History is full of geniuses who died unknown and frauds who were celebrated in their own day, which lends the statement an immediate plausibility.
It claims that the greatness of individuals can be judged only by those who come after them, never by their contemporaries.

Posterity certainly enjoys advantages of perspective that the present lacks, but the word only overstates the case, because contemporaries often recognize greatness clearly, and later generations bring distortions of their own.
It is true that time confers a clarity the present cannot have.
Contemporaries are swept up in fashions, rivalries, and prejudices that make a fair judgment difficult.
Van Gogh sold almost nothing in his lifetime, and Mendel's discoveries in genetics were ignored for decades before later scientists grasped their importance.
Only after the noise of an era fades can the lasting value of a person's work be weighed against everything that came before and after.
Many a politician adored in office looks small a century later, while quiet figures overlooked at the time loom large.
A reputation needs time to be tested against changing tastes, rival claims, and the eventual verdict of results.
In this sense the statement captures something real: distance can reveal what proximity hides.
However, to say that only posterity can judge is to ignore how often greatness is recognized in its own time.
Shakespeare was celebrated by his contemporaries, Newton was honored across Europe in his lifetime, and Lincoln was mourned by millions who already sensed his stature.
The people who actually witness a discovery, a performance, or an act of leadership often grasp its power more vividly than those who later read about it.
A scientist's peers are frequently the best placed of all to judge the importance of her work, since they alone fully understand the problem she solved.
Audiences who wept at a symphony's premiere were not mistaken about its power simply because they happened to live too early to be objective.
Contemporary judgment is not always wrong; it is merely incomplete, as every judgment is.

sections.role: Body — Posterity has its own biases

sentences.text: Moreover, later generations are not the impartial jury the statement imagines.
Each age rewrites the past to suit its own values, elevating figures it finds useful and burying those who have fallen out of fashion.
A reputation can rise and fall many times across the centuries, so posterity delivers not a single final verdict but an endless series of revisions.
If contemporaries are biased by being too close, descendants are biased by being too far, judging across a gulf of changed assumptions they barely notice.
The final judgment of history is really just the opinion of whichever age happens to be speaking at the moment.
There is no privileged vantage point from which greatness is seen plainly and forever.
In conclusion, the statement is right that time adds perspective but wrong to make posterity the sole judge.
Greatness is assessed in a long conversation between an age and all the ages that follow, each correcting the others without any reaching the final word.
Greatness, in the end, is less a fixed fact to be discovered than a reputation continually argued over.
We should trust neither the applause of the present nor the verdict of the future entirely, but listen, with appropriate humility, to both.
